title: Social Media
short: Ask before posting photos of others or their children, don't announce other people's news, and remember that posts are public and lasting.
trouble: Learners post a group photo or a friend's engagement news before the people in it have shared it themselves.

blocks.html: Social media is messaging with an audience. A post can reach hundreds of people, including some you never meant it for, and it can last for years.
Ask before posting photos of others or their children. Don't announce other people's news. Remember that posts are public and lasting.

A photo or a piece of news belongs, in part, to the people in it. A friend may not want a photo seen by an employer, or may want to tell family about an engagement or a pregnancy in their own words before the world knows. Asking first gives them that choice. And because posts can be copied and found later, writing only what you would be glad to see quoted keeps both you and others safe from embarrassment.

opts.title: Book club

messages.text: Loved tonight! Thanks for hosting, Priya.
Same! The lemon bars were perfect.
Big news: Hana and Omar are engaged!! I'm posting it everywhere!

opts.why: Hana and Omar's engagement is their news to share, in their own time and way.

blocks.cap: Spot the message that is not polite.

blocks.title: A group photo
blocks.q: After a hike, Mia wants to post a photo of the whole group. What should she do first?
steps: The photo includes friends who may not want it public.
She asks in the group chat: "Okay if I post this one?"
If anyone says no, she posts a different photo or none.

blocks.title: Someone else's news
blocks.q: James hears at work that his friend Nora got a promotion. Nora hasn't announced it. Should he post congratulations?
steps: It is Nora's news to announce.
He congratulates her privately and lets her share it when she is ready.
blocks.a: Congratulate her privately; let her announce it.
